# 2 Maccabees Chapter 14 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 14 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_014_page_001.jpg

---

**14:1** Three years later, word reached Judas and his men: Demetrius son of Seleucus had sailed into the harbor at Tripolis with a powerful army and a fleet.

**14:2** He had seized the throne, killing Antiochus and his guardian Lysias.

**14:3** There was a man named Alcimus who had formerly been high priest. He had deliberately defiled himself during the period of forced assimilation and now had no way back — no path to safety, no way to get near the holy altar again.

**14:4** In the 151st year he came to King Demetrius, bringing a gold crown, a palm branch, and some of the customary olive branches from the temple. He said nothing that day.

**14:5** But he waited for the right moment to advance his scheme. When Demetrius invited him to join the royal council and asked him about the intentions and disposition of the Jews, he spoke up:

**14:6** "The Jews who call themselves Hasideans — whose leader is Judas Maccabeus — are waging constant war and fomenting unrest. They won't let the kingdom settle down.

**14:7** I have been stripped of the honor of my ancestors — I mean the high priesthood — and that is why I am here.

**14:8** Partly because I genuinely care about the king's interests, and partly because I care about my own countrymen — because the foolishness of the men I mentioned is causing serious trouble for our whole nation.

**14:9** I urge you, Your Majesty, to learn the facts and then take action for the sake of our country and our people, who are besieged from every side — with the gracious goodwill you show to everyone.

**14:10** For as long as Judas is alive, there will be no peace for the government."

**14:11** His words were just what the king's other advisors needed. Those who already hated Judas immediately fanned Demetrius's anger higher.

**14:12** The king promptly appointed Nicanor — former commander of the elephants — as governor of Judea, and sent him off

**14:13** with orders to kill Judas, scatter his followers, and install Alcimus as high priest of the great temple.

**14:14** The Gentiles throughout Judea who had been running from Judas now came streaming to Nicanor, thinking the Jews' misfortune would be their gain.

**14:15** When the Jews heard that Nicanor was coming and that the Gentiles were gathering, they threw dust on their heads and prayed to the one who had established his people forever and who always defends his inheritance with his appearing.

**14:16** On their leader's command, they marched out immediately and confronted the enemy at a village called Dessau.

**14:17** Simon, Judas's brother, had engaged Nicanor's forces but suffered a temporary setback when the enemy appeared suddenly and unexpectedly.

**14:18** All the same, Nicanor had heard about the valor of Judas and his men — how fiercely they fought for their country — and he held back from forcing a bloodbath.

**14:19** Instead he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to arrange a truce and exchange pledges of friendship.

**14:20** The terms were worked out carefully, the leader laid them before the whole force, and when it became clear that everyone was in agreement, they accepted the covenant.

**14:21** They arranged a day to meet privately. A seat was brought forward from each side; they took their places.

**14:22** Judas had stationed armed men at key positions, ready for any sudden treachery. The meeting was conducted with appropriate formality.

**14:23** Nicanor remained in Jerusalem and did nothing untoward; he dismissed the mobs that had gathered around him.

**14:24** He kept Judas constantly at his side. He was genuinely fond of the man.

**14:25** He urged him to get married and start a family. Judas did marry, settled into ordinary life, and enjoyed the common pleasures of living.

**14:26** But Alcimus could see how close they had become. He got hold of the agreements they had made and went to Demetrius, accusing Nicanor of disloyalty — claiming he had appointed Judas, an enemy of the state, as his successor in Jewish affairs.

**14:27** The king erupted. Taken in by the slanders of this vile man, he wrote to Nicanor in a fury, stating that he was displeased with the agreements and demanding that Maccabeus be sent to Antioch in chains without delay.

**14:28** When the letter reached Nicanor, it shook him. He was deeply troubled that he would have to break his word to a man who had done nothing wrong.

**14:29** But he had no choice but to obey the king. He watched for an opportunity and looked for some way to carry out the order without direct confrontation.

**14:30** Maccabeus noticed the change. Nicanor was growing distant, more abrupt, less friendly than before in their meetings. Judas concluded that the coldness meant nothing good. He gathered a large number of his men and slipped away, going into hiding from Nicanor.

**14:31** When Nicanor realized the man had outsmarted him completely, he went to the great and holy temple while the priests were at their regular sacrifices. He ordered them to hand Judas over.

**14:32** They swore they had no idea where he was.

**14:33** Nicanor raised his right hand toward the sanctuary and swore: "If you do not deliver Judas to me as a prisoner, I will tear this shrine of God to the ground, demolish the altar, and build a magnificent temple to Dionysus right here."

**14:34** Then he left. The priests stretched out their hands to heaven and appealed to the one who always fights for our nation:

**14:35** "Lord of all, you need nothing — yet you chose to have your dwelling among us in this temple.

**14:36** Holy One, Lord of all holiness, keep this house — so recently purified — undefiled forever."

**14:37** A man named Razis — one of the elders of Jerusalem — was denounced to Nicanor. He was deeply loved by his fellow Jews, a man of reputation, who was called "father of the Jews" because of his devotion to his people.

**14:38** In the earlier days, when there was no forced mixing with Gentiles, he had been put on trial for being Jewish. He had offered up body and soul with total dedication to the Jewish cause.

**14:39** Nicanor wanted to demonstrate his contempt for the Jews in the most public way possible. He sent more than five hundred soldiers to arrest Razis.

**14:40** He calculated that taking this man would be a crushing blow to the Jews.

**14:41** When the troops were about to seize the tower — forcing open the courtyard gate, calling for fire to burn down the doors — Razis found himself completely surrounded. He drew his sword

**14:42** and chose to die with honor rather than fall into the hands of these criminals and endure humiliations that were unworthy of his noble character.

**14:43** In the chaos and the rush, he missed the stroke. The crowd was pouring in through the doors. He sprinted to the wall and threw himself off into the crowd below.

**14:44** They scattered quickly, and he landed in the empty space between them.

**14:45** Still breathing, still burning with spirit, he hauled himself to his feet. Blood was pouring out of his wounds in streams. He pushed through the crowd. He climbed to the top of a sheer rock.

**14:46** Now nearly bled dry, he tore out his own entrails and hurled them with both hands into the crowd. Then, calling on the Lord of life and spirit to give them back to him one day, he died.
